headline_en: Pension and gratuity for expatriate 'remittance fighters' is a demand of the time
summary_en: A reader's opinion piece (Dur Parabas section, 20 Jan 2025) argues that Bangladeshi migrants who send remittances have no pension, health care or social protection from the state when they return. It proposes a pension fund built from a small share of remittances, foreign-currency access to the Universal Pension Scheme, investment support, health and life insurance, a national representative body and education benefits for migrants' children.

facts.statement: The opinion writer states that about 1.5 crore (15 million) Bangladeshi expatriates send remittances and that the money they send is more than 7-8 percent of Bangladesh's GDP; no source is given.

The opinion writer claims that Bangladeshi migrant workers have no social protection system, no retirement guarantee and no help in times of danger from the state, and no financial protection after retirement.

Proposal by the opinion writer: create a central pension fund by keeping a small part of the remittances expatriates send, and open Bangladesh's Universal Pension Scheme (sarbojonin pension scheme) to expatriates' participation in foreign currency.

Proposals by the opinion writer: a transparent and safe system for expatriates to invest their savings with tax breaks and special incentives; a special health-care and life-insurance package valid both in Bangladesh and abroad, with health care for their families; a strong national body to represent expatriates at policy level; and special education opportunities and scholarships in Bangladesh for expatriates' children.

headline_en: How certificates of students going abroad are attested online
summary_en: Verification and attestation of SSC and HSC certificates, academic transcripts and mark sheets for students going abroad is now done online through an application module on the Ministry of Education website. The ministry posted a QR code for the link on its verified Facebook page on 11 December 2024. Online attestation began on 1 October 2024 and replaces the ministry's earlier 'One Stop Service'.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh government decided to do attestation of public-examination certificates online to reduce the suffering of people going abroad; the activity started on 1 October (2024), and as a result people no longer have to run to the Ministry of Education with the original copies of certificates.

Verification and attestation of SSC and HSC certificates, academic transcripts and mark sheets for students going abroad is done online: the applicant enters the online application module on the (Ministry of Education) website and completes the application. On Wednesday 11 December 2024 the Ministry of Education published a QR code of the link in a post on its verified Facebook page.

Order of document verification for going abroad as described in the article: an education certificate is first attested by the Ministry of Education, then by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, then by the embassy of the destination country, after which it is valid in that country.
For countries that have no embassy in Bangladesh, certificates have to be submitted for attestation at those countries' embassies in Delhi, which the article says causes great complication.

Two years before December 2024 the Secondary and Higher Education Division of the Ministry of Education had opened a 'One Stop Service' to reduce the attestation hassle for students going abroad; with online attestation started, that service is no longer needed.

headline_en: Saudi Arabia to take Bangladeshi nursing specialists; salary 95 thousand, medical care and airfare included
summary_en: BOESL (Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited) advertised 15 male and 15 female BSc nursing specialist posts at Afras Trading and Contracting Company in Saudi Arabia. The notice sets salary at SAR 3,000 a month with food allowance, housing, transport, primary medical care and airfare paid by the employer, and a BOESL service charge of BDT 56,350 plus other fees. The application deadline was 30 December 2024.

facts.statement: Through Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL), Afras Trading and Contracting Company in Saudi Arabia is to recruit 15 male and 15 female Nursing Specialists (BSc) from Bangladesh.

Eligibility for the BOESL Saudi nursing specialist posts at Afras Trading and Contracting Company: a BSc Nursing certificate from a government-approved nursing institute, a Prometric pass certificate, at least three years' experience in the relevant work, ability to communicate in English, and age within 40 years.
Monthly salary for the BOESL Saudi nursing specialist posts is BDT 95,315 (3,000 Saudi riyal), plus BDT 9,532 (300 Saudi riyal) per month for food.

Contract terms for the BOESL Saudi nursing specialist posts: 8 hours' duty a day, 6 days a week; two-year contract, renewable; three-month probation; 21 days' annual leave; the company bears accommodation, transport to the workplace and primary medical costs; the company pays the airfare for joining and for returning home at the end of the job; other benefits apply under Saudi law.

Selected candidates for the Saudi nursing specialist posts must pay BOESL's service charge of BDT 56,350 and, as per rules, other fees (GAMCA medical fee, visa stamping fee and other incidental fees), to be deposited at the respective offices.
Applicants for the BOESL Saudi nursing specialist posts had to apply by filling in a prescribed online form through a link given in the notice; the last date to apply was 30 December 2024.

headline_en: 82 more expatriate Bangladeshis return home from Lebanon
summary_en: 82 Bangladeshis returned from war-hit Lebanon on an Emirates flight that landed in Dhaka at about 11 pm on Thursday 21 November 2024; 76 were flown at government cost and 6 with IOM funding. By that date 697 Bangladeshis had returned from Lebanon on 11 flights. The government says it will bring back at its own cost everyone who wants to return.

facts.statement: 82 expatriate Bangladeshis returned from war-torn Lebanon on an Emirates Airlines flight that landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka at about 11 pm on Thursday 21 November 2024; 76 were sent back at Bangladesh government cost and 6 with IOM funding.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Foreign Affairs press release

facts.statement: Of the 82 Lebanon returnees of 21 November 2024, the 76 flown at government cost had registered at the Bangladesh Embassy in Beirut and the other 6 had registered with IOM. The return was supported by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, the Bangladesh Embassy in Beirut and the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

headline_en: Licences of 6 lakh drivers stuck
summary_en: BRTA (Bangladesh Road Transport Authority) has failed to print driving-licence smart cards for more than 6.25 lakh applicants, some waiting three years, because contractor Madras Security Printers of India has not supplied enough cards. The worst hit are people who want to go abroad as workers with a licence, because they cannot go without the smart card; some pay brokers large sums to get one. The interim government has decided to replace smart cards with PVC cards for new applicants.

facts.statement: More than 6.25 lakh (625,000) people who have paid and passed the test are waiting for BRTA (Bangladesh Road Transport Authority) to print their driving-licence smart cards; some have waited three years.

Because it cannot give smart cards on time, BRTA gives applicants a paper licence which traffic police accept, but people who want to go abroad as workers with a driving licence are the worst sufferers because without the smart card they cannot go abroad.

According to sources, small batches of driving-licence smart cards are now brought in and given to influential bureaucrats and people going abroad; to get one, a person going abroad has to be listed at the office of the BRTA chairman by showing the visa. Many do not know this, and there are allegations that those who know have to pay large sums.
facts.source_in_article: unnamed sources quoted by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: A 'syndicate' of local staff of Madras Printers and some BRTA officials is reported to have formed, printing some licences for extra money by exploiting the card shortage.
facts.source_in_article: unnamed sources quoted by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Abdul Matin of Cumilla, who holds a Saudi Arabia visa, applied to have his driving licence corrected by paying BDT 13,000 through a broker; the card had been waiting for printing for two months, and he will submit his passport to the embassy only once he gets the licence.
Fuzayel Ahmed, owner of a visa-processing service firm in Paltan, Dhaka, said many of his clients wait for licences and some have collected a licence through a broker at a cost of BDT 50,000.

The interim government decided to abolish the driving-licence smart card and give an ordinary plastic PVC card instead; according to BRTA sources PVC cards go to new applicants, while old applicants must be given the earlier card with no certainty of when. The PVC card will also carry a QR code to verify the licence on the road.
facts.source_in_article: BRTA sources; senior secretary Md. Ehsanul Haque, Road Transport and Highways Division

facts.statement: Madras Security Printers of India signed a contract with BRTA on 29 July 2021 to supply 40 lakh driving-licence smart cards by July 2026 at BDT 300.66 per card, got the work order in September 2021 and started supplying about six months late; by October 2024 it had supplied about 20 lakh cards and could not deliver cards for 6.25 lakh customers whose data it had taken. Its manager Ahmed Kani claimed BRTA does not pay bills on time; BRTA officials questioned the firm's capacity.
facts.source_in_article: BRTA sources; Ahmed Kani; BRTA officials

facts.statement: A 2021 survey by Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) found 83.1 percent of households were victims of corruption when getting a driving licence and 83.7 percent took the service through a broker or other intermediary.
Road transport adviser Muhammad Fouzul Kabir Khan told journalists on 18 August 2024 that his own driver had to take leave seven times to get a driving licence.

headline_en: 54 Bangladeshis return home from Lebanon in first batch
summary_en: On Monday 21 October 2024 the first batch of 54 Bangladeshis, including 7 children, returned from Lebanon on a Saudi Airlines flight because of the war with Israel. Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul said about one lakh Bangladeshis are in Lebanon, 1,800 had asked to return, and the government will bear the cost of bringing back all who wish to return, with IOM flying 200 at its own cost. IOM gave each of the 54 returnees food aid and BDT 5,000.

facts.statement: The first batch of 54 expatriate Bangladeshis, including 7 children, returned from Lebanon because of the war on Monday 21 October 2024; their Saudi Airlines flight landed (at Dhaka) at 5:55 pm. Another 65 were due to return on Wednesday (23 October 2024).

Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul said the interim government is taking all initiatives to bring Bangladeshis back from Lebanon, the government will bear the cost of bringing them back, and everyone who wants to return will be brought home; the government is working with IOM's cooperation to return them free of cost.
facts.source_in_article: Asif Nazrul, adviser, Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, press conference at Dhaka airport CIP lounge

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul said about one lakh (100,000) Bangladeshi expatriates are in Lebanon, of whom 1,800 had expressed a wish to return home; the number may rise or fall.
Asif Nazrul said BDT 17 crore 55 lakh had already been spent on assistance to Bangladeshis in Lebanon, of which 55 lakh was for food aid, and that IOM would bring 200 people at its own cost.

IOM gave each of the 54 Bangladeshis who returned from Lebanon on 21 October 2024 food assistance and BDT 5,000, plus psychological support; IOM is also working to bring back Bangladeshis in Lebanon who have no valid papers.
facts.source_in_article: Nusrat Ghazzali, acting chief of mission, IOM Bangladesh

facts.statement: Returnee Mohammad Hossain said four or five buildings next to the building where he lived in Lebanon were flattened, Israeli planes fly overhead all the time, and no place in Lebanon is safe; he had spent 15 days at the seaside with his wife and child before returning.

headline_en: Visa problem of Italy-bound workers to be resolved soon
summary_en: On 12 September 2024 foreign secretary Md. Jashim Uddin said the backlog of pending visas for Bangladeshi workers going to Italy would be resolved soon, after meeting Italian ambassador Antonio Alessandro. Italy's foreign ministry has formed a special task force only for Bangladesh. The ambassador attributed the backlog to interference by organised criminal networks, fake documents and an unexpected rise in visa requests; a migration MoU between the two governments is proposed.

Italy's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has formed a special task force only for Bangladesh to solve the work-visa backlog; the Italian ambassador gave assurance that the work-visa problem would be solved in the shortest possible time.

headline_en: UAE has not stopped visas for Bangladeshi citizens: foreign minister
summary_en: On 24 July 2024 foreign minister Hasan Mahmud said the UAE ambassador in Dhaka confirmed that the UAE had taken no decision to stop visas for Bangladeshis, calling media reports of a hiring stop 'absolutely bogus'. The article notes that protests without permission are banned in the UAE, and that on 22 July 2024 a UAE court jailed 57 Bangladeshis for protesting in solidarity with the quota reform movement, with deportation after their sentences.

facts.statement: Foreign minister Hasan Mahmud said the UAE has taken no decision to stop visas for Bangladeshi citizens; the UAE ambassador in Dhaka confirmed this to a director general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on 24 July 2024. He called media reports that the UAE had stopped taking workers from Bangladesh 'absolutely bogus'.
Any kind of protest without permission is banned in the United Arab Emirates.

On 22 July 2024 a court in the UAE sentenced 57 Bangladeshis to prison for protesting (on Friday 19 July 2024, in solidarity with Bangladesh's quota reform movement): three to life imprisonment, 53 to 10 years each and one to 11 years. State news agency WAM said they will be deported after completing their sentences.
facts.source_in_article: Emirati news agency WAM; Khaleej Times

facts.statement: On Saturday 20 July 2024, the day after expatriate Bangladeshis protested in the UAE, the Bangladesh Embassy in Abu Dhabi and the Bangladesh Consulate General in Dubai issued statements calling on expatriates to refrain from such activities.

headline_en: Malaysia labour market: High Court orders updated report every three months on action against mismanagement
summary_en: On 16 July 2024 a High Court bench ordered the authorities to submit every three months an updated report on steps taken against mismanagement that left workers unable to travel to Malaysia after getting final clearance. The court also issued a rule asking why inaction against those responsible should not be declared illegal and why victims' deposited money should not be returned with profit and compensation paid. The writ was filed on 3 June 2024 by Supreme Court lawyer Tanvir Ahmed.

facts.statement: A High Court bench of Justice Mustafa Zaman Islam and Justice S M Masud Hossain Dolon on Tuesday 16 July 2024 ordered that an updated report on steps and activities taken against mismanagement in sending workers to Malaysia after final clearance be submitted to the court every three months, and issued a rule.

The High Court rule asks why the inaction and indifference of the authorities in taking immediate steps against those involved in ruining the lives of victims (workers who could not go to Malaysia after final clearance) should not be declared illegal, and why an order should not be given to return the money victims deposited to go to Malaysia with profit and later pay compensation.

Two newspaper reports of 2 June 2024 attached to the writ were headlined '20 thousand crore taka looted, breaking the dreams of 30 thousand youths' (a Bangla daily) and 'Jobs in Malaysia: more than three thousand workers did not get tickets due to mismanagement' (an English daily).
facts.source_in_article: newspaper reports cited in the writ

facts.statement: Supreme Court lawyer Tanvir Ahmed filed the writ on 3 June 2024, seeking a three-member independent inquiry committee led by an additional secretary of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment. It came up on 30 June 2024, when the court asked the state to report what action had been taken; on 15 July 2024 the state presented information from the report of a six-member inquiry committee, and on 16 July Deputy Attorney General Tushar Kanti Roy presented parts of the inquiry report, its recommendations and action taken on them.

named_actors.name: Tanvir Ahmed
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Supreme Court lawyer who filed the writ over workers unable to fly to Malaysia after final clearance.

headline_en: If you want higher education in Saudi Arabia
summary_en: An explainer on Saudi university scholarships for Bangladeshi students. Bangladeshis must first enter a university's Arabic language institute (a Diploma in Arabic of up to two years) before starting a bachelor's course. It lists age and GPA conditions, scholarship benefits (about SAR 840 a month, no tuition, free housing and medical care, yearly ticket), the documents and attestation chain, the mahram requirement for female applicants, and four universities.

facts.statement: To study in Saudi Arabia a Bangladeshi student must first be admitted to a university's Arabic language institute and apply for the Diploma in Arabic; after satisfactory results there, the student can enter a bachelor's course. Bangladeshi students cannot apply directly to bachelor's programmes at Saudi universities. All Saudi universities that admit foreign students have an Arabic language institute.

The four-level Diploma in Arabic at Saudi universities takes two years in total; those with good Arabic can start directly from level two or three and finish in one to one and a half years before starting the bachelor's course.

At Saudi universities, bachelor's courses in Arabic and Islamic subjects (Shariah, Dawah, Islamic Studies) are taught entirely in Arabic, while bachelor's courses in all other subjects are taught in English; every student, whatever the subject, must study basic Arabic and Islamic studies.

Conditions for Saudi university scholarship applicants from Bangladesh: age 17 to 23 (25 at some universities) and a minimum GPA of 4 in HSC/Alim; some universities do not state the result requirement clearly and some accept applications with GPA below 4.00.

Saudi university scholarship benefits: monthly stipend of about 840 Saudi riyal, no tuition fee, free accommodation and medical care, a three- to four-month summer vacation, a return ticket home once a year and a preparation allowance; some universities provide family visas and quarters for married students. The article says all education in Saudi Arabia is free and all educational materials are supplied free.

Documents for a Saudi university scholarship application (each as a PDF of at most 200 KB): passport valid at least two years; passport-size photo on white background without cap or glasses; medical fitness certificate from a civil surgeon or any medical centre; HSC/Alim certificate and mark sheet translated into Arabic by an approved translation centre, notarised and attested by the Islamic Foundation, then attested by the relevant education board, the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and finally by the Saudi Embassy in Bangladesh.

Further documents for a Saudi university scholarship application: a character certificate from the applicant's country's Islamic Foundation or two distinguished Islamic scholars or a college teacher; for a hafez, the hifz certificate translated into Arabic and notarised; some universities also ask for Arabic-translated and notarised citizenship and birth registration certificates.

Female applicants to Saudi universities need a copy of the iqama of their mahram guardian; the article says that under Saudi Arabia's Islamic constitution women are not permitted higher education there without a mahram.

Saudi universities listed in the article as admitting foreign students: Islamic University of Madinah (Madinah), King Abdulaziz University (Jeddah), Umm Al-Qura University (Makkah) and Taibah University (Madinah).

headline_en: Four workers abducted in Libya; ransom demanded with torture videos
summary_en: Four men from Charpara village, Gurudaspur upazila, Natore, who went to Libya two years earlier, were abducted and tortured; on 2 June 2024 videos of the torture were sent to their families with a demand of BDT 10 lakh each. The workers told their families the abductors are Bangladeshis. Each had spent about BDT 4 lakh to go; the families are afraid to file a police complaint.

facts.statement: Four workers from Charpara village, Biaghat union, Gurudaspur upazila, Natore - Sohan Pramanik (20), Sagor Hossain (24), Nazim Ali (36) and Bidyut Hossain (26) - who went to Libya two years earlier were abducted and tortured more than a week before 7 June 2024; on 2 June 2024 torture videos were sent to their families and BDT 10 lakh ransom per person was demanded.

Abductors in Libya called a victim's father on the imo app while the son was being tortured and screaming, threatened to kill him unless BDT 10 lakh was paid, then showed video of him tied up in a room with three others. The abducted workers told their families that the abductors are Bangladeshis.

Each of the four Natore workers spent BDT 4 lakh to go to Libya, raised by mortgaging land, selling cattle and borrowing; over two years each family received on average BDT 2 lakh in money sent home, and the loans were not yet repaid.

Gurudaspur police station OC Ujjal Hossain said the families were advised to file a complaint at the police station but are afraid to do so for fear of the abductors; the matter was reported to the Natore superintendent of police. The Biaghat union parishad chairman Mizanur Rahman also advised them to go to the police.
facts.source_in_article: Ujjal Hossain, OC Gurudaspur; Mizanur Rahman, UP chairman

headline_en: Honesty, accountability, competence all nearly extinct in the country
summary_en: A column by lawyer Dr. Shahdeen Malik (3 June 2024) on corruption and the loss of democracy. It cites a 30 May 2024 Prothom Alo report that recruiting agencies of four members of parliament, part of the Malaysia 'syndicate', sent seven to eight thousand migrants to Malaysia at more than BDT 5 lakh each against a rule-set cost below BDT 80,000. He adds that people now pay BDT 18-20 lakh to flee via Iran, Libya and the Mediterranean.

facts.statement: According to a Prothom Alo report of 30 May 2024 headlined on four MPs' booming business after entering the 'ring', recruiting agencies of four members of parliament sent seven to eight thousand migrants to Malaysia; the MPs are not named in this column.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Shahdeen Malik citing Prothom Alo, 30 May 2024

facts.statement: By rule the migration cost per person for Malaysia is below BDT 80,000, but because of the recruiting agencies' syndicate each Malaysia-bound migrant spent more than BDT 5 lakh - which the columnist calls a 7-8 fold increase over the set price.
facts.source_in_article: columnist Shahdeen Malik citing Prothom Alo, 30 May 2024

facts.statement: The columnist writes that people now want to flee Bangladesh via 'Iran-Turan-Libya-the Mediterranean' even at a cost of BDT 18-20 lakh.

headline_en: Demand for easy-term loans for women returned from abroad
summary_en: At a press conference at the National Press Club on 29 May 2024, the Centre for Women and Children Studies (CWCS), supported by Manusher Jonno Foundation, presented a policy review on returned women migrant workers. It asked the government for a separate rehabilitation project, career counsellors, a separate database, free legal aid and guarantor-free loans of BDT 1 to 3 lakh on the basis of migration papers only.

facts.statement: CWCS (Centre for Women and Children Studies) said returned women migrant workers face many risks: most people do not look on them favourably and in some cases the husband or family does not want to take them back; it demanded a separate government project to rehabilitate helpless returned women workers and career counsellors to advise those who want to start a business.
facts.source_in_article: CWCS policy review, press conference at National Press Club

facts.statement: CWCS recommended loans of BDT 1 to 3 lakh for returned women migrant workers without any guarantor, on the basis of migration-related papers only; migrant service centres at people's doorstep; a separate database of returned women workers; and free legal assistance through government legal aid for victims of sexual exploitation, torture, forced labour or trafficking.
CWCS ran a project on empowerment of returned women migrants in two upazilas of Dhaka, Keraniganj and Nawabganj, from 2020 to 2023, arranging various work for them through training.
CWCS formed an alliance called Nari Obhibashi Kontho (Women Migrants' Voice) in 2022 with 22 organisations working on women migrants; it has 25 member organisations as of May 2024.

named_actors.what_the_article_says: NGO that presented the policy review on returned women migrant workers; president Ishrat Sharmin (ইশরাত শারমিন) and member Farida Yasmin presented the paper.

headline_en: How they traffic people to India with job offers and take their kidneys
summary_en: Dhaka Metropolitan Police say a ring took poor people to India with promises of jobs, held them in Delhi and took their kidneys; ten people have been trafficked this way. After victim Robin filed a case at Dhanmondi police station, three members were arrested on 11 and 12 May 2024 in Dhanmondi and Bagerhat. Robin was promised BDT 6 lakh, had a kidney removed in a Gujarat hospital on 4 March 2024, and his wife was given BDT 3 lakh.

facts.statement: A ring recruited poor people in Bangladesh with promises of a job in India, took them to Delhi, held them hostage and took a kidney. In victim Robin's case, absconding accused Masum overheard him talking about money troubles at a tea stall behind Shah Ali Market, Mirpur-10, Dhaka in April 2023, said he had a business in India and could give him a job, and kept in regular phone contact until he agreed.
facts.source_in_article: DMP additional commissioner (Crime and Ops) Mohid Uddin, press conference 12 May 2024

facts.statement: The kidney ring told victim Robin that medical tests were needed to go to India, took him to a hospital in Dhaka in September (2023) where he was introduced to Raju Hawlader, took his passport for a visa after the health check, and after the visa introduced him to Shahed and Atahar as business partners trading in Bangladesh and India; he was then taken to Delhi.

Victim Robin was first taken to the Faridabad area of Delhi, given kidney-related tests at a hospital in New Delhi, then kept in a house in the Muktinagar area of Gujarat; on 4 March (2024) the accused, using threats, had one kidney removed by surgery at a hospital in Gujarat. He was discharged after four days and then held at an unknown place for 10-11 days.
facts.source_in_article: Dhanmondi police; DMP additional commissioner Mohid Uddin

facts.statement: The kidney ring told Robin he would get BDT 6 lakh under the deal but gave BDT 3 lakh after taking the kidney: ring members in Bangladesh handed BDT 3 lakh to his wife, after which he returned home. In hospital he learned the accused had sold his kidney to a broker ring for a large sum.

After victim Robin filed a case at Dhanmondi police station, police arrested three ring members in raids in Dhanmondi and Bagerhat on Saturday 11 and Sunday 12 May 2024: Md. Raju Hawlader (32), Shahed Uddin (22) and Md. Atahar Hossain Bappi (28). Absconding in the case are Md. Masum (27), Shahin (35), Sagor alias Mostafa (37) and others, 10-12 in all.
Dhaka Metropolitan Police said the ring has so far trafficked 10 people to India and taken their kidneys.

headline_en: A large part of the remittance incentive is going into the bellies of big fish
summary_en: At the third A K N Ahmed memorial lecture at BIBM, Mirpur, on 7 March 2024, former Bangladesh Bank governor Mohammed Farashuddin said a large part of the government's remittance incentive goes to big players and middlemen, who pass only part to remitters and bring the rest by illegal channels. Governor Abdur Rouf Talukder said anyone declaring dollars on arrival will not be questioned and can deposit them in an RFCD account. Farashuddin urged a single exchange rate that absorbs the incentive.

facts.statement: Former Bangladesh Bank governor Mohammed Farashuddin said a large part of the incentive the government gives on remittances goes to 'big fish' and middlemen, who give part of the incentive to those sending remittances and take the rest themselves, bringing money through illegal channels; because of this remittances did not grow as much as expected.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammed Farashuddin, A K N Ahmed memorial lecture, BIBM

facts.statement: Bangladesh Bank governor Abdur Rouf Talukder said that if someone coming from abroad declares that they have brought dollars, no one will question them, and those dollars can be deposited in a bank RFCD (Resident Foreign Currency Deposit) account.
facts.source_in_article: Abdur Rouf Talukder, Bangladesh Bank governor

facts.statement: Governor Abdur Rouf Talukder said that after Bangladesh Bank simplified the process of depositing dollars in banks, on average USD 5 lakh in cash is being deposited every day, and banks ask no questions.

Farashuddin said Bangladesh no longer needs multiple exchange rates and should have a single rate into which the remittance incentive is merged. The governor replied that a year earlier there were separate dollar prices for exports, imports and remittances but no longer; banking-sector people said the fixed dollar price is mostly not effective and dollars are traded at higher prices.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammed Farashuddin; Abdur Rouf Talukder; banking-sector sources

key_quote_bn: আবার বিদেশ থেকে আসার সময় কেউ যদি ঘোষণা দেয় আমি ডলার নিয়ে এসেছি, কেউ প্রশ্ন করবে না।

headline_en: 9,370 Bangladeshis held in prisons of 26 countries
summary_en: Foreign minister Hasan Mahmud told parliament on 19 February 2024 that 9,370 Bangladeshis are held in prisons in 26 countries, the most in Saudi Arabia (5,746), with 508 in Turkey. Since July 2023, 1,226 were repatriated from Libya, 51 from prisons in France and other European countries, and about 1,950 from prisons in India, Myanmar and Middle Eastern countries.

facts.statement: Foreign minister Hasan Mahmud told the Jatiya Sangsad that 9,370 Bangladeshis are held in prisons in 26 countries: Portugal, Egypt, Italy, South Africa, South Korea, Sri Lanka, Qatar, Libya, Spain, Hong Kong, Singapore, Brunei, China, United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Algeria, Thailand, Lebanon, Greece, Iraq, Turkey, Myanmar, Japan and Jordan.
facts.source_in_article: Hasan Mahmud, foreign minister, in parliament

facts.statement: Of the 26 countries, Saudi Arabia's prisons hold the most Bangladeshis, 5,746; 508 are held in Turkey.
facts.source_in_article: Hasan Mahmud, foreign minister, in parliament

facts.statement: From July 2023 to 19 February 2024, 1,226 Bangladeshis were repatriated from Libya and 51 from prisons in France and other European countries; in addition about 1,950 Bangladeshis were brought back from prisons in India, Myanmar and various Middle Eastern countries.
facts.source_in_article: Hasan Mahmud, foreign minister, in parliament

facts.statement: Bangladesh maintains diplomatic relations through 81 embassies; it has 17 own embassy buildings in 14 countries and owns land in 7 countries.
facts.source_in_article: Hasan Mahmud, foreign minister, in parliament

facts.statement: More than eight lakh (800,000) British-Bangladeshis live in the United Kingdom, according to the foreign minister.
facts.source_in_article: Hasan Mahmud, foreign minister, in parliament

headline_en: 454 Bangladeshi garment workers in Jordan receive unpaid wages and benefits
summary_en: 454 Bangladeshi garment workers laid off in December 2023 from a factory named 'Asil' (আছিল) in Al Tajamouat near Amman received their unpaid wages, leave pay and social security money through the Bangladesh Embassy in Amman on Tuesday 30 January 2024. The embassy worked with Jordan's labour ministry, the ILO and trade unions. Jordan's labour ministry said the workers would start being sent home from Sunday 4 February 2024.

facts.statement: 454 Bangladeshi garment workers in Jordan received their arrears of wages and allowances and social security money, handed over through the Bangladesh Embassy in Amman on Tuesday (30 January 2024). They had worked at a garment factory named 'Asil' (আছিল) in the Al Tajamouat area near Amman and were laid off in December (2023), the company citing business losses.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo Dur Parabas report; Bangladesh Embassy in Jordan

facts.statement: Worker Md. Motahar said he received six months' unpaid salary, payment for five years of earned leave and social security money from the Jordan garment factory settlement.

Bangladeshi workers at the Jordan factory complained to the Bangladesh Embassy from late 2022 about unpaid wages and other issues; the embassy sat in talks with the factory authorities, with cooperation from Jordan's Ministry of Labour, the ILO and trade unions. First secretary (labour) Umme Salma said the embassy tried for one and a half years; the article elsewhere says the problem was solved after more than two years of talks (the two durations differ in the article).
facts.source_in_article: Umme Salma, first secretary (labour), Bangladesh Embassy in Jordan

facts.statement: Woman worker Karima Akter said many of the laid-off workers' passports had expired and some had lost their passports, and the Bangladesh Embassy in Jordan solved all these problems.
Jordan's Ministry of Labour said the 454 Bangladeshi garment workers who received their dues would start being sent home from Sunday 4 February 2024.

headline_en: Malaysia to review agreements on taking workers from Bangladesh
summary_en: Malaysia announced it will review its bilateral foreign-worker agreements with 15 countries including Bangladesh, to stop labour exploitation and balance manpower across sectors. Human resources minister Steven Sim said five firms accused of promising jobs to hundreds of workers and not providing them have been investigated, employers must pay wages whether or not there is work, and 751 Bangladeshi workers have filed wage claims of about BDT 5.11 crore with the labour department.

facts.statement: Malaysia announced it will review bilateral foreign-worker agreements with 15 countries including Bangladesh, as part of efforts to stop labour exploitation and ensure a balance of manpower across sectors; recruitment fees, other costs, contract clauses, health and related matters will be reviewed.
facts.source_in_article: Malaysian human resources minister Steven Sim and home minister Saifuddin Ismail, speaking to journalists on Tuesday

facts.statement: In 2023 several thousand foreign workers who went to Malaysia, mostly from Bangladesh and Nepal, found no jobs and fell into distress; some Malaysian firms had falsely promised them jobs if they paid more than the government-set recruitment fee, but they got no jobs after arriving.

Malaysian minister Steven Sim said employers who hired such workers must pay their wages whether or not there is work, and companies and individuals who break the law will not be allowed to hire migrant workers; authorities had completed investigation of five firms accused of promising jobs to hundreds of workers and not giving them.
facts.source_in_article: Steven Sim, Malaysian human resources minister

facts.statement: 751 Bangladeshi migrant workers have filed cases with Malaysia's labour department claiming owed wages of about BDT 5 crore 11 lakh (at 1 ringgit = BDT 23.26).
facts.source_in_article: Steven Sim, Malaysian human resources minister

facts.statement: Malaysian ministers said manpower in various industrial firms has exceeded the set quota while agriculture and forestry still have a labour shortage; the home minister said the government will also allow transfer of workers between sectors according to quota.
More than 70 percent of foreign workers in Malaysia are from Bangladesh, Indonesia and Nepal; the remaining 30 percent are from India, Vietnam, Pakistan and Thailand.
The United States imposed bans on several Malaysian companies in recent years over forced labour allegations; many workers allege they were paid no wages at all.

headline_en: 'I want to see my son's face one last time'
summary_en: Sourav Majhi (23) of Majhikandi village, Naria, Shariatpur, died in the early hours of Sunday (about 14 January 2024) after falling from a building in 'Rolla city' in the UAE while trying to jump to the next building when police raided. He had worked as a painter in Sharjah for a company that did not pay regularly and had recently moved to Rolla. His family wants the government to bring the body home; the UNO said the embassy will be contacted.

facts.statement: Bangladeshi worker Sourav Majhi (23) of Majhikandi, Noshason union, Naria upazila, Shariatpur died in the early hours of Sunday after falling from a building in Rolla city (রোলা শহর), UAE: police raided a building where he and two friends were staying, and he fell while jumping to an adjacent building to escape; a local hospital doctor declared him dead.

Sourav Majhi went to the UAE in 2021 (elsewhere the article says two years before January 2024) and worked as a painter in Sharjah; the company he worked for did not pay wages regularly, so he had moved from Sharjah to Rolla some days before his death. His cousin said his visa was still valid and the family does not understand why he fled Sharjah.

The family learned of Sourav Majhi's death on Tuesday 16 January 2024 from a relative in the UAE. The Noshason union parishad chairman Delwar Hossain Talukdar asked the UNO to arrange return of the body; Naria UNO Shankar Chandra Baidya said it was not known where the body was, but an initiative would be taken to bring it home by contacting the embassy there.
facts.source_in_article: Delwar Hossain Talukdar, UP chairman; Shankar Chandra Baidya, UNO Naria

headline_en: Gunfight between joint forces and traffickers in Teknaf, 8 rescued
summary_en: At about 12:30 am on the night of Saturday 21 November 2026, joint forces led by the army's Ramu 10 Infantry Division raided a traffickers' den at Lengurbil, Teknaf Sadar union, Cox's Bazar, where 70-80 men and women had been gathered for trafficking by sea. Traffickers fired while fleeing by boat and took most of the people with them; 5 women, 2 men and 1 child were rescued. No one was hurt.

The traffickers escaped taking most of the people with them, but 5 women, 2 men and 1 child were rescued and handed to Teknaf Model police station, where their identities are to be confirmed.

headline_en: Note in Pagla Mosque donation box: 'Make a place for me in Swarna's heart'
summary_en: When the 15 donation chests of Pagla Mosque in Kishoreganj were opened on 21 November 2026, 51 sacks of money and a sack of letters were found. One anonymous letter, signed 'a cheated person bound for abroad', says the writer was cheated by a broker over a dream of going to Europe and prays for justice and a safe journey. The rest of the article is about other notes and the donation count and has no migration content.

facts.statement: Among letters found in the Pagla Mosque donation chests in Kishoreganj, one person wrote of being cheated by a broker while dreaming of going to Europe, of the money lost, and prayed for justice against the fraudsters, for embassies and visa services of all European countries to be available in Bangladesh, and that no one going abroad be cheated by brokers; the writer signed as 'a cheated person bound for abroad'. No names, amounts or countries are given.
facts.source_in_article: anonymous letter described by Prothom Alo

headline_en: 11 directives for medical centres on health tests of Malaysia-bound workers
summary_en: Workers have started health tests to go to Malaysia, and 51 medical centres have been approved from Malaysia to run them. On Thursday 19 November 2026 the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment issued 11 directives to the centres: a fixed fee of BDT 8,000 with nothing extra, no money in the name of 'MiGRAMS', medical slips limited to the demand-letter number plus 5 percent, no repeated or fake tests, and the centre bears all costs if a worker declared fit is found unfit in Malaysia.

facts.statement: Workers have started taking health tests to go to Malaysia; 51 medical centres (in Bangladesh) have been approved from Malaysia to conduct these tests.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment notice

facts.statement: The fixed fee for the health test of Malaysia-bound workers is BDT 8,000 and medical centres may not collect any amount above it; no money may be collected in the name of 'MiGRAMS' (মাইগ্রাম, Malaysia's worker recruitment software).
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment notice

facts.statement: If a Malaysia-bound worker declared fit in the health test in Bangladesh is declared unfit in a health test after reaching Malaysia, up to the point of being placed in employment, the medical centre must bear all costs related to the worker, including the cost of sending the worker back home.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment notice

facts.statement: Medical slips for Malaysia-bound workers must be issued on the basis of the number of workers in the demand letter sent by the Malaysian employer; at most 5 percent more slips than that number may be issued, and a medical centre may not issue slips beyond the limit of its own will or to send extra workers.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment notice

facts.statement: Medical centres may not deliberately declare the same Malaysia-bound worker unfit and make them take the test repeatedly without need, and may not make, give or use any fake or forged medical report.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment notice

facts.statement: Each approved medical centre must prepare and keep a detailed person-by-person report of each day's tests and submit test reports online to the ministry with the worker's name, passport number, visa number and other information; must have all modern equipment, follow internationally recognised standards, have enough seating, and put up a large visible billboard in front of its entrance.
facts.source_in_article: Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment notice

facts.statement: If a medical centre for Malaysia-bound workers breaks the conditions, its security deposit will be forfeited and its licence cancelled, along with other legal action; the ministry will form a strong monitoring team to watch compliance strictly.

headline_en: Execution of two Bangladeshis in Makkah: Bangladesh did not know beforehand, letter sent to Saudi Arabia seeking information
summary_en: Bangladesh learned only from media that two Bangladeshis, named as Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhter, were executed in Saudi Arabia for 'immoral' acts in a mosque area in Makkah; the Saudi Press Agency confirmed it on Wednesday 14 October 2026. The Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah wrote to the Saudi foreign ministry on Thursday 15 October asking for details. The sentence was a discretionary 'taazir' punishment under Shariah, upheld by a higher judicial authority and carried out by royal order.

facts.statement: The Saudi Press Agency (SPA), citing the Saudi interior ministry, confirmed on Wednesday (14 October 2026) that death sentences were carried out on two Bangladeshi nationals for 'immoral' acts in a mosque area in Makkah; those executed are reported to be Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhter.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi Press Agency; Prothom Alo sources

facts.statement: According to Gulf News, Saudi security forces arrested the two Bangladeshis on the allegation of engaging in immoral and indecent acts in a mosque in Makkah; after preliminary investigation they were charged and sent to court, which sentenced them to death under 'taazir', the judge's discretionary punishment under Shariah law, considering the violation of the mosque's sanctity and the circumstances; a higher judicial authority upheld the verdict and a royal order directed that it be carried out.
facts.source_in_article: Gulf News, cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The Saudi interior ministry said in a statement that it stands firm on protecting the security of the holy mosques and enforcing Shariah law against violators of religious sanctity, and warned that repetition of such crimes in holy places will face severe punishment.

A source at the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah said Saudi authorities did not formally inform Bangladesh before carrying out the executions; Bangladesh learned from media reports, and on Thursday 15 October 2026 the Jeddah consulate sent a letter to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs requesting details.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah source; Foreign Ministry sources in Dhaka

facts.statement: Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia are both parties to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations; under its Article 36, when a national is arrested abroad the detaining country must, at the prisoner's request, inform that person's consulate without delay and allow consular assistance. It is not yet clear whether the two prisoners asked for the consulate to be informed.

Unofficial sources in Saudi Arabia said the trial of the two Bangladeshis had been going on for several months in a Jeddah court and two distinguished Bangladeshi citizens helped as interpreters during it. Foreign Ministry officials, speaking anonymously, said it is not expected that Saudi authorities detained and executed them very quickly, and called it mysterious that no one contacted the mission on their behalf.
facts.source_in_article: unofficial sources in Saudi Arabia; unnamed Foreign Ministry officials

facts.statement: No information was yet available on the type and duration of the two executed Bangladeshis' stay in Saudi Arabia or on whether any legal assistance or appeal was used in the trial.

people_cases.outcome: Executed; confirmed by SPA on 14 October 2026; Bangladesh was not informed beforehand

headline_en: Where is the law or rule that an unmarried woman cannot go abroad
summary_en: Three adult women with valid passports, visa or entry permission and air tickets were stopped at Bangladesh airport immigration on their way to visit Nepal, allegedly because they were unmarried and travelling on their own. After a complaint to the additional inspector general of police got no response they filed a writ, and on 29 September 2026 the High Court issued a rule. Sakia Haque of Travelettes of Bangladesh argues no Bangladeshi law bars unmarried women from travelling abroad.

facts.statement: Three adult women travelling to Nepal as tourists allege that Bangladesh airport immigration stopped them despite valid passports, visa or entry permission and air tickets: officers asked whether their families knew, told them to phone home (which they did), and asked why they were going on their own while unmarried.
facts.source_in_article: the three women, as reported by Prothom Alo and Sakia Haque

facts.statement: The three women complained to the additional inspector general of police asking for an investigation and action; getting no response they filed a writ, and on 29 September 2026 the High Court issued a rule asking why stopping the three women from travelling abroad should not be declared to be without lawful authority.

Article 36 of Bangladesh's Constitution recognises a citizen's right to leave and re-enter Bangladesh, subject to reasonable restrictions set by law; Article 28 provides for equal rights of women and men and non-discrimination by the state on grounds of sex.
facts.source_in_article: Sakia Haque, co-founder, Travelettes of Bangladesh

facts.statement: Under the Bangladesh Passport Order, 1973 no one can leave the country without a valid passport or travel document, and a passport can be refused, restricted or cancelled on specific legal grounds; the writer says it contains no separate prohibition on 'unmarried women'.
facts.source_in_article: Sakia Haque, co-founder, Travelettes of Bangladesh

facts.statement: The writer says women leaving Bangladesh have for years faced irrelevant immigration questions such as 'Are you married?', 'Your husband let you go alone?' and 'Where do you get so much money?'; a 'gender equity' component she and Manoshi Saha worked on in immigration police training some years ago has, she has heard, been discontinued.

people_cases.what_happened: Stopped at Bangladesh airport immigration despite valid passport, visa/entry permission and tickets; asked whether family knew and made to phone home.
people_cases.outcome: Filed a writ; High Court issued a rule on 29 September 2026

headline_en: 'Singapore Silent Heroes' award winner Sakib Hossain and finalist Raihan Sarkar
summary_en: Bangladeshi migrant Sakib Hossain of Lohagara, Chattogram won the Compassionate Foreigner category of the 13th Singapore Silent Heroes award (2026), presented on 19 September 2026 at Shangri-La Singapore; Raihan Sarkar of Daudkandi, Cumilla was a finalist. Both volunteer for migrant workers' health, safety and skills; Raihan founded the volunteer platform 'We Care SG' in 2023 and advises migrants on career development including 'WPLN'.

facts.statement: Expatriate Bangladeshi Sakib Hossain of Barahatia, Lohagara, Chattogram won the 'Compassionate Foreigner' category of the 13th 'Singapore Silent Heroes' award (2026), presented on 19 September at Shangri-La Singapore with law minister Edwin Tong as chief guest; Raihan Sarkar of Gopalpur village, Daudkandi, Cumilla was a finalist. One winner is chosen in each of five categories from 20 finalists.

Raihan Sarkar founded a volunteer platform of expatriates called 'We Care SG' in Singapore in 2023; through it members donate blood, clean the homes of elderly and helpless local people, clean beaches, and he advises expatriates on career development including 'WPLN'. He is studying, alongside work, for a BSc related to health, safety and risk management at Robert Gordon University (RGU), UK.

Sakib Hossain, alongside his job in Singapore, has advised migrant workers on health awareness, drug awareness, workplace safety and upgrading skills, and volunteers in blood donation and beach clean-ups.
